# Backup Restore Drill

## Overview

A drill is the only real proof that a backup works. Reading job logs tells me the copy finished; it does not tell me the archive opens, the permissions survived, or that I can find the token that unlocks it at eleven at night. So twice a year, in spring and again in autumn, I clear a Saturday morning, wheel the spare laptop out of the cupboard, and rebuild a machine from nothing. That spare is an old ThinkPad with a tired battery and a good screen. It exists for this job, and for the odd evening when the main machine is in pieces on the bench. It never holds live data, so wrecking it costs me nothing. The point of the drill is not the laptop. The point is that my hands remember the sequence, and that I discover the missing step on a quiet weekend instead of during an outage. I write down the time I start and the time the rebuilt machine reaches its login screen, and I file both figures next to the checklist. Twice a year is often enough to keep the routine fresh and rare enough that I do not resent losing the morning. The drill has caught two genuine problems so far, and neither of them showed up in any log. The first was a missing key that had been on a machine I had long since replaced; the second was a permissions change that no job had reported. Neither would have been visible until the night I actually needed the data, which is the worst possible night to find either. That is the whole argument for the drill. It converts a quiet concern into a short morning of honest work, and it leaves a number behind that I can compare against.

## Steps

First I clear the desk completely, because a restore always needs more room than I expect for a keyboard, a USB hub, and a second drive, and I read the printed checklist from beginning to end before I touch anything. That printed page is the whole point of the exercise. I read it slowly, aloud sometimes, and I mark each line as I go. Only after that do I plug the spare laptop in and start the work. The clearing takes longer than it sounds, because the desk collects receipts and cables through the winter, and a cluttered desk is exactly when I drop a small stick behind the drawer and lose ten minutes.

I boot the rescue USB first. The stick holds a small live Linux and the client tools needed to reach the archive host, so the spare laptop can talk to the storage box before any operating system is installed. I check the date on the stick once a year and refresh it, because a rescue image from three years ago can no longer read a modern filesystem and I would not know until I tried. The boot takes under a minute on the old hardware, though the wireless does not come up on this particular image, so I plug in a cable. That is written on the checklist, which is how I know it.

Next I pull the latest snapshot. The archive host holds the most recent copy of the desktop, so I fetch the newest one rather than reaching for an older set out of habit. I note the snapshot timestamp on the checklist. If the newest snapshot is more than a day old, that is itself a finding, and I stop and investigate before restoring anything. An old snapshot usually means a job has been failing quietly, which is the sort of thing the drill is designed to catch. I also check the size of the snapshot against the last one I restored, because a set that has shrunk by half is a warning, not a saving.

Then I restore the home directory first, ahead of the system. That order matters to me. The home tree is where all the irreplaceable work lives, the images, the writing, the notes and the keys. If the morning runs short I want the valuable half finished rather than the half I can reinstall easily from a package manager. I unpack the home tree to a fresh path on the spare laptop and watch the counter climb. I resist the strong urge to check my email while it runs, because the counter is the only thing worth watching and I want to see it move.

Once the home tree lands I restore the system. That covers the operating system, the packages listed in my manifest, and the handful of configuration files under the system directories. The manifest is a plain text list I keep beside the checklist, and it rebuilds the same set of tools every time. I let the restore run and I resist the urge to tinker while it works, since every hand on the keyboard during a restore is a chance to break something that would otherwise have finished.

Now I compare the file counts. I run `find . -type f | wc -l` inside the restored home tree and compare it with the count I recorded at the last drill. The two figures should match closely. A gap of a few files is normal, because I have added work since that record. A gap of hundreds means something did not come across, and I chase it down before I go further. I also count the image directory and the document directory separately, since those are the two trees that matter most to me. If the image count is short I look at whether a recent import is missing, because that is the usual reason.

Then I open a sample of images and a document. Numbers alone can lie, so I click through half a dozen photographs and confirm they decode and look right, and I open one long document and scroll to its end. I check that the metadata survived and that the filenames are intact. I look at the dates on a few files too, because a restore that brings back the right names with the wrong dates is a restore I would rather know about now. Once I have done that I check permissions. I look at the ownership and the mode on a few directories and files and confirm they match what the live machine had. A restore that brings back the bytes but hands everything to the wrong user is a restore I would have to fix by hand, and finding that out on a Saturday is far better than finding it out in a crisis.

Finally I time it. I record the total from the first command to the first login prompt, and I note it beside the older figure. The whole drill took 90 minutes door to door, which is a little slower than the year before, mostly because the old laptop's drive is the slow part. I write that number down and I stop for the day. I do not tidy the desk until the notes are written, because the notes are the thing I actually keep, and a tidy desk with no notes is a wasted morning.

## Notes

The printed checklist lives in a drawer, in a plastic sleeve, and it is the first thing I reach for. It has grown margins full of pencil marks over four drills. What surprised me the first time was how much of the work was not the restore at all. Half the morning disappeared into finding the right USB stick and remembering which command read the archive, not into copying data. So after the second drill I added a fresh rescue stick to the drawer and pinned the two commands to the top of the checklist. I also learned to write the snapshot timestamp down as I go, because I cannot remember it twenty minutes later. The change I made afterwards was small and dull. I now keep the manifest and the checklist in the same sleeve, so I never start a restore without both in my hand. I also made the spare laptop log in without a password prompt for the local account, since typing a long passphrase on a laptop I use twice a year was a silly way to lose five minutes. The other change was to stop restoring into a path I had used before, because a stale directory left over from an earlier drill made the file count look better than it really was, and I nearly recorded the wrong figure. Now each drill restores into a path named after the date, so the count is honest and the old tree cannot flatter it.

## Troubleshooting

A snapshot that will not mount is usually a missing key or a stale client. I check the passphrase first, then the tool version, then whether the archive host is actually reachable at all. A wrong password costs me a minute if the passphrase lives in the password manager, and an hour if I am guessing, which is why the entry sits at the top of the entry list with a name I can find. A drive that reports errors mid-restore is the nastier case. If the target disk starts throwing read or write errors while I am writing to it, I stop immediately, take a different spare drive out of the cupboard, and start again rather than push through a failing medium. Restoring onto a bad disk just spreads the damage and wastes the morning. I keep one spare small SSD on the shelf for exactly this, and it has saved one drill so far. I also keep the archive passphrase written on a slip of paper in the same drawer, sealed in an envelope, for the case where the password manager itself is the thing that is unavailable. That sounds paranoid until the day the manager will not sync, and on that day the paper is the difference between a morning of work and a morning of guessing. I check the envelope once a year to confirm the passphrase still works, since a sealed envelope nobody has opened is not much better than no envelope at all.
